title: Mandible and orbital floor fractures

guidelineVersions: BAOMS/GIRFT. Isolated Fractured Mandible Pathway (last updated April 2022)
BAOMS/GIRFT. Isolated Fractured Zygomatic Complex/Orbit Pathway (last updated April 2022)
Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th edition (2023)

related.why: Major trauma primary survey, into which assessment of facial injuries fits
Neck triangles, parotid gland and facial nerve anatomy, relevant to facial trauma assessment

brief.scenario: Mr Daniel Whitcombe, 31, is brought in after an assault with facial swelling, malocclusion and diplopia.
brief.task: Assess his injuries, interpret the CT findings the examiner reads out, and explain your management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Life-threatening trauma first, then mandible assessment, then orbital assessment (vision is the priority), then imaging and referral.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Assuming diplopia and facial swelling are just expected after an assault, without formally assessing vision.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd first assess for life-threatening trauma, particularly airway compromise and associated head or cervical-spine injury."

flow: Assess for orbital injury, vision first

grid.label: Exclude life-threatening trauma first (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Goes straight to examining the face without first considering airway compromise or associated head/cervical-spine injury.
grid.pass: Assesses for life-threatening trauma first, particularly airway compromise and associated head and cervical-spine injury.
grid.high: Specifically asks about loss of consciousness and neurological symptoms and checks cranial nerves before focusing on the facial injury alone.

grid.label: Mandibular fracture assessment
grid.fail: Notes only visible swelling without assessing occlusion, mandibular movement or sensation.
grid.pass: Assesses occlusion, mandibular movement, dentition, intraoral wounds, sensation in the mental nerve distribution and facial symmetry.
grid.high: Explains that malocclusion is a clinically useful clue to a mandibular fracture and helps judge restoration of normal occlusion after treatment.

grid.label: Orbital assessment, vision first (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Says diplopia does not matter, or does not assess vision because the injury is described as "just a fracture".
grid.pass: Assesses visual acuity, pupils, eye movements, diplopia, globe position and signs of optic nerve injury.
grid.high: States that visual assessment is never skipped in facial trauma, because a fracture can coexist with a vision-threatening globe or optic nerve injury.

grid.label: Interpret the CT findings
grid.fail: Cannot interpret the CT findings as an orbital floor fracture or describe why it threatens the globe or extraocular muscles.
grid.pass: Interprets the CT findings as an orbital floor fracture and explains the mechanism by which it can cause diplopia (extraocular muscle or fat entrapment) or globe malposition.
grid.high: Links the CT findings to specific findings on examination (for example entrapment correlating with restricted upward gaze) rather than interpreting the CT in isolation.

grid.label: Imaging and specialist referral
grid.fail: Ignores the CT findings, arranges plain radiographs only and discharges, without urgent maxillofacial or ophthalmology referral.
grid.pass: Interprets the CT and acts on it: urgent maxillofacial and ophthalmology referral for suspected inferior rectus entrapment.
grid.high: Adds that associated zygomatic, nasal or skull-base injury should be considered and looks for a CSF leak.

grid.label: Recognise vision-threatening complications (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Treats all orbital injuries the same regardless of visual findings, or delays referral despite acute visual loss.
grid.pass: Recognises that an orbital injury with visual loss, severe globe displacement or evidence of orbital compartment syndrome requires urgent specialist intervention.
grid.high: States clearly that urgent treatment of threatened vision is never delayed for other, less urgent aspects of facial trauma management.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What injuries are you concerned about?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Facial swelling is expected after an assault, so I wouldn't worry too much yet.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What would you examine for the jaw?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Diplopia doesn't really matter here — it's just a fracture.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Here are his CT findings. What do they show?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Something in the orbit is broken, but I'm not sure what it means or why it matters.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I wouldn't treat this any differently whatever his vision shows.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What injuries are you concerned about?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd first assess for life-threatening trauma, particularly airway compromise and associated head and cervical-spine injury.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What would you examine for the mandible?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Occlusion, mandibular movement, dentition, intraoral wounds, sensation in the mental nerve distribution and facial symmetry.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Visual acuity, pupils, eye movements, diplopia, globe position and signs of optic nerve injury.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Here are his CT findings. What do they show?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: There's an orbital floor fracture, which can cause diplopia through extraocular muscle or fat entrapment, or through globe malposition.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd act on the CT now: urgent maxillofacial and ophthalmology referral, as this looks like inferior rectus entrapment.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: An orbital injury with visual loss, severe globe displacement, or orbital compartment syndrome requires urgent specialist intervention.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What injuries are you concerned about?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: First excluding life-threatening trauma, including airway compromise and head or cervical-spine injury — I'd also ask about loss of consciousness and check cranial nerves before focusing on the face alone.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What would you examine for the mandible?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Occlusion, mandibular movement, dentition, intraoral wounds, mental nerve sensation and symmetry — malocclusion is a clinically useful clue to the fracture and helps me judge whether normal occlusion is restored afterwards.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Vision first, always — acuity, pupils, eye movements, diplopia, globe position and optic nerve signs — because a facial fracture can coexist with a vision-threatening injury that's easy to miss if I stop at the bone.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Here are his CT findings. What do they show?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: An orbital floor fracture — I'd correlate that with his examination, so if he has restricted upward gaze that fits with extraocular muscle entrapment at this fracture site rather than reading the CT on its own.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd act on the CT now: urgent maxillofacial and ophthalmology referral for suspected inferior rectus entrapment, and I'd also look for associated zygomatic, nasal or skull-base injury and check for a CSF leak.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Visual loss, severe globe displacement or orbital compartment syndrome need urgent specialist intervention, and I would never let that be delayed by managing the less urgent parts of his facial trauma first.

failures.move: Dismissing diplopia as unimportant in a facial fracture.
failures.consequence: A vision- or muscle-threatening orbital injury can be missed until damage is established.

failures.move: Not escalating urgently despite visual loss or severe globe displacement.
failures.consequence: Delayed specialist intervention risks permanent visual loss from orbital compartment syndrome or optic nerve injury.

failures.move: Focusing on the visible facial injury before excluding airway compromise or head/cervical-spine injury.
failures.consequence: A life-threatening associated injury can be missed while attention is on the face.

failures.move: Ignoring the CT findings and relying on plain radiographs, then discharging without urgent maxillofacial or ophthalmology referral.
failures.consequence: Orbital or mandibular injuries requiring specialist repair are missed or treated too late.

recovery.when: You blank on what to do next
recovery.line: I'd like to structure this around immediate safety, assessment, escalation and definitive management.

recovery.when: Asked "anything else?" after the facial examination
recovery.line: Yes — I'd also consider associated zygomatic, nasal or skull-base injury and a CSF leak.

knowledge.fact: Malocclusion is a clinically useful clue to mandibular fracture and helps assess restoration of normal occlusion after treatment.
Orbital assessment always includes visual acuity, pupils, eye movements, diplopia and globe position, because vision can be threatened even when the injury looks like "just a fracture".
Acute visual loss or signs of optic nerve/orbital compartment compromise make an orbital injury immediately vision-threatening and needs urgent specialist intervention.
When CT facial bones shows an orbital floor fracture with suspected inferior rectus entrapment, refer urgently to maxillofacial surgery and ophthalmology.

recall.think: Vision-threatening orbital injury or airway/cervical-spine trauma hiding behind facial swelling.
recall.say: "Excluding life-threatening trauma first, then assessing vision before anything else on the face."
do: Exclude airway/C-spine and head injury first
Occlusion, mandibular movement, sensation for the jaw
Visual acuity, pupils, eye movements, diplopia for the orbit

numbers.value: Acuity, pupils, eye movements, diplopia, globe position
numbers.meaning: Minimum orbital examination set before assuming an orbital fracture is straightforward

recall.trap: Assuming diplopia or facial swelling are just expected after trauma and not formally assessing vision.
recall.finish: Act on the CT: urgent maxillofacial and ophthalmology referral; urgent intervention if vision is threatened.

partner.opening: Mr Daniel Whitcombe, 31, is brought in after an assault with facial swelling, malocclusion and diplopia. "Assess his injuries, interpret the CT findings I will read out, and explain your management."

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about loss of consciousness or neurology
reveals.finding: No loss of consciousness; GCS 15, cervical spine clinically clear.

reveals.trigger: Candidate assesses occlusion and mandibular movement
reveals.finding: Malocclusion with a step deformity and reduced mouth opening.

reveals.trigger: Candidate assesses vision and eye movements
reveals.finding: Visual acuity is preserved but he has restricted upward gaze and diplopia on upward gaze.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for imaging, or the examiner reaches the CT question
reveals.finding: Read out: coronal CT of the facial bones shows a break in the thin floor of the left orbit, with the bony fragment displaced downwards into the roof of the left maxillary sinus. The inferior orbital rim is intact. Soft tissue of fat density, together with the lower edge of the inferior rectus muscle, hangs through the defect into the sinus as a teardrop-shaped opacity. The right orbit is normal.

push.question: Why is malocclusion important?
push.expect: It is a clinically useful clue to mandibular fracture and helps assess restoration of normal occlusion.

push.question: What finding makes the orbital injury immediately vision-threatening?
push.expect: Acute visual loss or other signs of optic nerve/orbital compartment compromise.

push.question: What do the CT findings show, and why do they explain his diplopia?
push.expect: Orbital floor fracture with muscle or fat entrapment or globe malposition restricting eye movement.

curveballs.prompt: He suddenly develops severe pain, a tense proptotic eye and reduced acuity.
curveballs.safeAnswer: This suggests orbital compartment syndrome — urgent specialist intervention is needed, not routine referral.

curveballs.prompt: A colleague suggests just repeating plain radiographs and reviewing in clinic.
curveballs.safeAnswer: No — the CT already shows an orbital floor fracture with suspected inferior rectus entrapment, so urgent maxillofacial and ophthalmology referral is needed now.

curveballs.prompt: He also has clear fluid trickling from one nostril.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider a CSF leak and associated skull-base injury, and involve the appropriate specialists.
